lessons.title: Parts of the Body
lessons.body: In Shona, the body is called 'muviri'. Start by learning the head, 'musoro'. Your eyes are 'maziso', ears 'nzeve', nose 'mhuno', and mouth 'muromo'. For the torso, 'mudumbu' is the stomach, 'chipfuva' is the chest, and 'musana' is the back. Arms are 'maoko', hands 'maoko' (same word), fingers 'minwe', and legs 'makumbo'. Feet are 'tsoka', and toes are 'zvigunwe'. When you visit a clinic in Harare or Bulawayo, the nurse might ask, 'Unorwadziwa kupi?' meaning 'Where does it hurt?' You can reply, 'Musoro unorwadza' (My head hurts) or 'Mudumbu unorwadza' (My stomach hurts). Practice pointing to each part on your own body as you say the word aloud. For example, touch your head and say 'musoro', touch your eyes and say 'maziso'. This method helps you remember faster. Also, learn the plural forms: 'maziso' (eyes), 'nzeve' (ears), 'maoko' (arms/hands), 'makumbo' (legs). In everyday conversation, you might hear 'Ane maziso akanaka' (She has beautiful eyes). To ask about someone's health, you can say, 'Muviri wako wakanaka here?' (Is your body well?). If you are in a rural area and need to explain a pain to a traditional healer, knowing these words is crucial. For instance, 'Baba, musoro wangu unorwadza uye ndine chizungu' (Father, my head hurts and I feel dizzy). Remember that Shona uses prefixes to show possession: 'wangu' means 'my', 'wako' means 'your', 'wake' means 'his/her'. So 'musoro wangu' is 'my head', 'musoro wako' is 'your head'. Practice with a friend: one points to a body part, the other names it in Shona. Do this for 10 minutes daily. Within a week, you will know all the major parts. This vocabulary is the foundation for describing any health issue, so master it first.

lessons.title: Common Illnesses and Symptoms
lessons.body: In Shona, common illnesses include 'chirwere' (disease), 'mukana' (flu), 'chikosoro' (cough), 'fivha' (fever), and 'kurwadziwa' (pain). Symptoms like headache are 'musoro unorwadza', stomach ache 'mudumbu unorwadza', and nausea 'kurutsa'. If you have diarrhea, say 'ndine manyoka'. For malaria, the word is 'marariya', and you might say 'ndine marariya' (I have malaria). A runny nose is 'mhuno inoyerera', and a sore throat is 'huro inorwadza'. When you feel weak, say 'ndine usimbe'. To ask someone if they are sick, say 'Uri kurwara here?' (Are you sick?). They might reply, 'Hongu, ndiri kurwara' (Yes, I am sick). In many African communities, people use herbal remedies like 'moringa' or 'mupfuti' for various ailments. For example, 'mupfuti' (moringa) is used to boost immunity. But it's important to know when to go to a clinic. If you have a fever above 38Â°C, go to the nearest health center. In Shona, 'fivha' means fever. You can say 'Ndine fivha' (I have a fever). Also, learn to describe duration: 'Ndakarwara kwemazuva maviri' (I have been sick for two days). 'Mazuva' means days. If you have a cough, say 'Ndine chikosoro'. For a cold, 'ndine dzihwa'. When you visit a pharmacy, you can ask for medicine: 'Ndinoda mushonga wechikosoro' (I need medicine for a cough). Remember that 'mushonga' means medicine. Common symptoms also include 'kurwadziwa nemusoro' (headache), 'kurwadziwa nemudumbu' (stomach ache), and 'kunzwa kuneta' (feeling tired). Practice these phrases with a partner. For instance, one person acts sick and says, 'Ndine fivha nechikosoro', and the other responds with advice: 'Enda kuchipatara' (Go to the hospital). This will help you communicate effectively when you or someone else is ill.

lessons.title: Visiting a Doctor or Pharmacy
lessons.body: When you visit a doctor in Zimbabwe, you might go to a 'chipatara' (hospital) or 'kiriniki' (clinic). A pharmacy is 'khemisiti' or 'chitoro chemishonga'. At the reception, you will be asked, 'Unoda kuona chiremba here?' (Do you want to see a doctor?). You can reply, 'Hongu, ndinoda kuona chiremba' (Yes, I want to see a doctor). The doctor is called 'chiremba' or 'dhokotera'. A nurse is 'mukoti'. When you see the doctor, they may ask, 'Uri kunzwa sei?' (How are you feeling?). You can say, 'Ndiri kunzwa kurwadziwa nemusoro' (I am feeling a headache). If you need medicine, the doctor will write a prescription, 'chinyorwa chemishonga'. You then take it to the pharmacy. At the pharmacy, say, 'Ndine chinyorwa chemishonga' (I have a prescription). The pharmacist might ask, 'Unoda mushonga uyu here?' (Do you want this medicine?). You can ask about dosage: 'Ndinofanira kunwa mushonga kangani pazuva?' (How many times a day should I take the medicine?). The answer might be 'Katatu pazuva' (Three times a day). Also, learn to say 'mangwanani' (morning), 'masikati' (afternoon), and 'manheru' (evening) to specify times. If you have allergies, say 'Ndine allergy kune penicillin' (I am allergic to penicillin). For payment, you might ask, 'Mushonga uyu unodhura zvakadii?' (How much does this medicine cost?). In rural areas, you might visit a 'n'anga' (traditional healer) first. But for emergencies, go to the clinic. Remember to bring your 'chitupa' (ID) and 'kadhi rehutano' (health card). If you don't understand, say 'Ndapota, dzokorora' (Please repeat). Practice these phrases with a friend to build confidence. Role-play a visit to the doctor: one plays the patient, the other the doctor. This will prepare you for real situations.

lessons.title: Describing Pain and Discomfort
lessons.body: To describe pain in Shona, use the verb 'kurwadza' (to hurt). For example, 'Musoro unorwadza' means 'My head hurts'. You can specify the type of pain: 'kurwadza kwakanyanya' (severe pain), 'kurwadza kushoma' (mild pain), 'kurwadza kunopisa' (burning pain), 'kurwadza kunotonhora' (dull pain). If the pain is sharp, say 'kurwadza kunocheka'. For a throbbing pain, 'kurwadza kunorova'. To say 'I feel pain in my chest', say 'Ndine kurwadziwa muchipfuva'. If you have a stomach ache, 'Mudumbu unorwadza'. For a headache, 'Musoro unorwadza'. You can also say 'Ndiri kurwadziwa' (I am in pain). To ask someone where it hurts, say 'Unorwadziwa kupi?' The answer might be 'Ndiri kurwadziwa musana' (I have pain in my back). If you feel dizzy, say 'Ndine chizungu'. For nausea, 'Ndine kurutsa'. If you have a fever, 'Ndine fivha'. To describe the intensity, use 'zvakanyanya' (very much) or 'zvishoma' (a little). For example, 'Musoro unorwadza zvakanyanya' (My head hurts very much). If the pain is getting worse, say 'Kurwadziwa kuri kuwedzera'. If it's getting better, 'Kurwadziwa kuri kupera'. You can also use similes: 'Kurwadziwa kunenge kuchibaya' (The pain is like stabbing). Practice by describing different scenarios: a headache, a backache, a toothache ('zino rinorwadza'). If you have a toothache, say 'Zino rangu rinorwadza'. To say 'I cannot sleep because of the pain', say 'Handikwanise kurara nekuda kwekurwadziwa'. These phrases will help you communicate clearly with a doctor or nurse. Remember to use gestures to show where it hurts. Combine words with pointing for effective communication.

lessons.title: Healthy Habits and Advice
lessons.body: In Shona, healthy habits are called 'tsika dzakanaka dzehutano'. To stay healthy, you should 'kudya zvinovaka muviri' (eat nutritious food), 'kunwa mvura yakawanda' (drink plenty of water), and 'kurovedza muviri' (exercise). Eat fruits and vegetables like 'muriwo' (vegetables), 'muchero' (fruit), and 'nyama' (meat) in moderation. Drink at least 8 glasses of water daily. In Shona, water is 'mvura'. Say 'Ndinonwa mvura yakawanda' (I drink a lot of water). Exercise is 'kurovedza muviri'. You can say 'Ndinoro vedza muviri mangwanani' (I exercise in the morning). Sleep is 'kurara'. Aim for 7-8 hours of sleep. Say 'Ndinorara maawa masere' (I sleep eight hours). Avoid alcohol and smoking: 'Usanwa doro' (Don't drink alcohol) and 'Usaputa fodya' (Don't smoke). To give advice, use 'unofanira' (you should). For example, 'Unofanira kudya michero' (You should eat fruits). To ask for advice, say 'Ndinofanira kuita sei kuti ndive neutano hwakanaka?' (What should I do to be healthy?). A common response is 'Idya zvinovaka muviri uye urove muviri' (Eat nutritious food and exercise). Also, washing hands is 'kugeza maoko'. Say 'Ndinogeza maoko' (I wash my hands). To prevent illness, 'Dzivirira chirwere' (Prevent disease). You can say 'Ndinoda kudzivirira chirwere' (I want to prevent disease). In many African communities, people use 'mishonga yechivanhu' (traditional medicine) alongside modern medicine. But always consult a professional. Practice these phrases with a friend. For instance, one says 'Ndine fivha' and the other advises 'Unofanira kunwa mvura yakawanda uye kuzorora' (You should drink plenty of water and rest). This will help you give and receive health advice in Shona.

lessons.title: Emergency Phrases
lessons.body: In an emergency, every second counts. Learn these Shona phrases to call for help. 'Ndapota, ndibatsireiwo!' means 'Please help me!' If someone is injured, shout 'Akakuvara!' (He/She is injured!). For a fire, 'Moto!' (Fire!). If someone is drowning, 'Ari kunyura!' (He/She is drowning!). To call an ambulance, say 'Fonera ambulance' (Call an ambulance). The emergency number in Zimbabwe is 994 for ambulance, 995 for fire, and 999 for police. But in rural areas, you might need to transport the person to the nearest clinic. Say 'Ndinoda kuti tiende kuchipatara' (I want us to go to the hospital). If someone is unconscious, 'Akapera simba' (He/She is unconscious). For bleeding, 'Ari kubuda ropa' (He/She is bleeding). To ask for a first aid kit, 'Ndinoda bhokisi rekurwara' (I need a first aid kit). If someone has a seizure, 'Ari kugwinha' (He/She is having a seizure). To say 'Call a doctor', 'Fonera chiremba'. If you are lost, 'Ndarasika' (I am lost). For a snake bite, 'Akarumwa nenyoka' (He/She was bitten by a snake). To say 'I need help urgently', 'Ndinoda rubatsiro nekukurumidza'. Practice these phrases with a partner. Role-play scenarios: one acts as the victim, the other as the rescuer. For example, victim: 'Ndapota, ndibatsireiwo! Ndine kurwadziwa muchipfuva!' Rescuer: 'Zorora, ndichafonera ambulance.' Also, learn to give directions: 'Kuchipatara kuri kure here?' (Is the hospital far?). If you need to describe the emergency, say 'Pane tsaona' (There is an accident). Remember to stay calm and speak clearly. These phrases can save lives.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Health & Body Language for Shona-Speaking Markets

For agribusiness operators, farm managers, extension officers, and traders working across Zimbabwe and the wider Shona-speaking belt, health vocabulary is not academic. It is operational. When a worker reports musoro unorwadza (headache) at 6 a.m., when a customer at a rural pharmacy asks for mushonga wechirwere chemudumbu (medicine for stomach illness), or when you must explain a workplace injury to a clinic nurse, the right Shona phrase protects productivity, reduces downtime, and builds trust with the communities your business depends on.

This Practical Reference consolidates the six lessons in the Health and Body module into a single working document. Use it as a laminated field card, a staff induction handout, or a quick-lookup page for supervisors who manage mixed-language teams. Every term is given in Shona with an English gloss, and where relevant, a note on the business scenario in which it is most useful.

Core Body-Part Vocabulary

The table below is the minimum viable vocabulary for a farm or factory first-aid conversation. It covers the parts most likely to be named in injury reports, insurance forms, and clinic intake interviews.

Table 1: Essential Shona Body-Part Terms for Workplace and Clinic Use
Shona English Business / Clinical Use
MusoroHeadHeadache reports, helmet fit, heatstroke checks
Meso / ZisoEyes / EyeChemical splash, dust exposure, PPE compliance
NzeveEar(s)Noise-induced hearing loss claims, machinery zones
MhunoNoseRespiratory irritation from pesticides or grain dust
MuromoMouthOral rehydration, ingestion incidents
MutsipaNeckManual handling injuries, tractor seat ergonomics
ChipfuvaChestChest pain triage, cardiac referral
DumbuStomach / AbdomenDiarrhoeal illness, food hygiene incidents
MusanaBackLifting injuries, the most common farm compensation claim
Ruoko / MaokoArm/Hand (sg/pl)Cut injuries, tool safety, hand-washing compliance
Gumbo / MakumboLeg(s)Mobility, snakebite, field transport planning
Tsoka / TsokaFoot / FeetBoot provision, puncture wounds, foot rot in livestock handlers
GandaSkinDermatitis, pesticide exposure, sun damage
RopaBloodBleeding control, first-aid kits, HIV/TB screening consent
PfupaBoneFracture reporting, referral urgency

Source: Compiled from Hannan, M. (1984), Standard Shona Dictionary (College Press, Harare), and the Ministry of Health and Child Care (Zimbabwe) community health worker training glossary, 2019 edition.

Common Illnesses and Symptoms

Agribusiness operations in Zimbabwe face a predictable illness profile: malaria in lowveld estates, bilharzia near irrigation schemes, diarrhoeal disease where sanitation is shared, and respiratory conditions in tobacco and cotton processing. Knowing the Shona symptom words lets a supervisor triage accurately before the clinic visit.

Table 2: Illness and Symptom Vocabulary with Operational Notes
Shona English Operational Note
ChirwereIllness / DiseaseGeneral term; use chirwere chipi? to ask "what illness?"
KurwadzaTo hurt / be painfulCore verb for any pain report
Musoro unorwadzaHeadacheCheck hydration and heat exposure first
Fivha / Kupisa muviriFever / Body heatMalaria screen if in endemic district
Kurutsa / KurutsaVomitingPesticide exposure red flag
ManyokaDiarrhoeaWater source audit; ORS distribution
ChikosoroCoughTB screening if >2 weeks; dust control review
Kupera simbaFatigue / WeaknessAnaemia, malaria, or overwork
KuzvimbaSwellingInjury, allergy, or infection
KurumaItchingDermatitis, scabies, allergic reaction
MarondaWounds / SoresInfection risk; first-aid protocol trigger
Chironda chemudumbuStomach ulcer / Abdominal painRefer if severe or recurring
ShuramatongoMalaria (colloquial)Mosquito net and prophylaxis compliance
ChindhomaBilharzia (schistosomiasis)Irrigation workers; avoid canal contact
Kushaya hopeInsomniaShift-work and stress indicator

Source: Symptom terminology cross-referenced with the World Health Organization's Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response technical guidelines (AFRO region, 2019) and Zimbabwe's National Health Strategy vocabulary list.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Emergency and Consent Language

Never rely on a single phrase in a medical emergency. If a worker is unconscious, bleeding heavily, has swallowed pesticide, or reports chest pain, call emergency services immediately (993 for ambulance in Zimbabwe, 112 from mobile networks across much of Southern Africa) and use the phrase "Ndapota, batsirai! Munhu uyu anoda chiremba." ("Please help! This person needs a doctor."). Do not attempt to obtain consent for treatment using Shona phrases unless you are a registered health professional â miscommunication in consent can create legal liability for your business. Keep a written EnglishâShona consent card prepared by a qualified translator, and ensure at least one supervisor per shift is trained in basic first aid and emergency Shona.

Visiting a Doctor or Pharmacy

In rural Zimbabwe, the first point of care is often a village health worker or a rural clinic, not a doctor. The pharmacy counter at a growth point is a commercial interaction as much as a health one. The following phrases keep that interaction efficient.

  • Ndinoda kuona chiremba. â I need to see a doctor.
  • Ndinoda mushonga wechirwere ichi. â I need medicine for this illness.
  • Mushonga uyu unonwiwa kangani pazuva? â How many times a day is this medicine taken?
  • Ndinorwadziwa pano. â I have pain here (point to the site).
  • Ndine fivha kubva nezuro. â I have had a fever since yesterday.
  • Ndinoda bara rechirwere. â I need a sick note / medical certificate.

For agribusiness managers, the sick note (gwaro rekurwara or bara rechirwere) matters for payroll and insurance. Train supervisors to request it politely and to log the clinic name, date, and diagnosis category. This protects both the worker and the business in any compensation dispute.

Describing Pain and Discomfort

Shona pain description is often metaphorical. Workers may say musoro unorova (my head is beating) for a throbbing headache, or dumbu rinopisa (my stomach is burning) for gastritis. Learn the metaphors, not just the dictionary words.

  • Inorwadza zvikuru. â It hurts a lot.
  • Inorwadza zvishoma. â It hurts a little.
  • Inorova. â It is throbbing / beating.
  • Inopisa. â It is burning.
  • Ndine chizungu. â I feel dizzy.
  • Ndinonzi ndinorutsa. â I feel like vomiting.
  • Handikwanise kufamba. â I cannot walk.
  • Handikwanise kusimuka. â I cannot stand up.

Healthy Habits and Advice

Health messaging in Shona lands better when it is framed around work capacity, not abstract wellness. A supervisor who says "Geza maoko nguva dzose kuti usarwara uye usarasikirwe nebasa" ("Always wash your hands so you don't get sick and lose work") is more persuasive than a generic hygiene poster.

  • Geza maoko nguva dzose. â Wash your hands regularly.
  • Nwa mvura yakawanda. â Drink plenty of water.
  • Rara nguva yakakwana. â Sleep enough.
  • Dya zvokudya zvine hutano. â Eat healthy food.
  • Shandisa mosquito net. â Use a mosquito net.
  • Enda kuchipatara kana uchinge usina kunaka. â Go to the clinic if you feel unwell.

Emergency Phrases

These phrases should be posted at every workstation, weighbridge, and packhouse. They are short enough to memorise under stress.

  • Batsirai! â Help!
  • Ndapota, fonera ambulance. â Please call an ambulance.
  • Munhu uyu akakuvara. â This person is injured.
  • Munhu uyu haafeme. â This person is not breathing.
  • Ndoda first aid kit. â I need the first-aid kit.
  • Ndoda chiremba nekukurumidza. â I need a doctor urgently.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Post a laminated ShonaâEnglish body-part and emergency phrase card at every workstation and first-aid point.
  2. Train at least one supervisor per shift in basic first aid and the emergency Shona phrases above.
  3. Keep a written, professionally translated consent card in the first-aid kit â do not improvise consent language.
  4. Record all injury and illness reports using both the Shona term given by the worker and the English clinical term.
  5. Verify the nearest clinic, pharmacy, and ambulance contact number for each operating site, and update quarterly.
  6. Include health vocabulary in staff induction so new hires can report symptoms accurately from day one.
  7. Audit water, sanitation, and PPE provision against the illness profile in Table 2 each season.
  8. Review sick-note and compensation procedures annually with a qualified HR or legal advisor.

Further Reading

  • World Health Organization â Health Topics (free, multilingual health guidance including African regional materials).
  • WHO Regional Office for Africa (free technical guidelines, disease surveillance, and community health resources).
  • Ministry of Health and Child Care, Zimbabwe (official national health policy, clinic directories, and public health notices).
  • International Labour Organization â Occupational Safety and Health (free guidance on workplace injury reporting and compensation).
  • FAO Africa â Agribusiness and Rural Health (free resources linking farm productivity to worker health and safety).

This Practical Reference is a language-learning aid, not medical advice. For clinical decisions, consult a registered health professional. For legal or compensation decisions, consult a qualified advisor in your jurisdiction.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'head'?
quiz.explanation: 'Musoro' means head, while 'maziso' means eyes, 'nzeve' ears, and 'muromo' mouth.

quiz.q: How do you say 'My stomach hurts' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Mudumbu' means stomach, and 'unorwadza' means hurts.

quiz.q: Which word means 'ears' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Nzeve' is the Shona word for ears.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'legs'?
quiz.explanation: 'Makumbo' means legs, while 'maoko' means arms/hands.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I have a fever' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Fivha' means fever, so 'Ndine fivha' means 'I have a fever'.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'cough'?
quiz.explanation: 'Chikosoro' means cough, while 'dzihwa' means cold.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I have diarrhea' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Manyoka' means diarrhea, so 'Ndine manyoka' means 'I have diarrhea'.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'malaria'?
quiz.explanation: 'Marariya' is the Shona word for malaria.

quiz.q: How do you ask 'Are you sick?' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Uri kurwara here?' means 'Are you sick?'.

quiz.q: What does 'mushonga' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Mushonga' means medicine, while 'chiremba' means doctor.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I want to see a doctor' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndinoda kuona chiremba' means 'I want to see a doctor'.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'pharmacy'?
quiz.explanation: 'Khemisiti' means pharmacy, while 'chipatara' is hospital.

quiz.q: How do you say 'three times a day' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Katatu' means three times, 'pazuva' means per day.

quiz.q: What does 'chiremba' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Chiremba' means doctor, while 'mukoti' means nurse.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am allergic to penicillin' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndine allergy kune penicillin' means 'I am allergic to penicillin'.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'pain'?
quiz.explanation: 'Kurwadziwa' means pain, while 'kurwadza' is the verb 'to hurt'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'My head hurts severely' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Zvakanyanya' means very much, so 'Musoro unorwadza zvakanyanya' means 'My head hurts severely'.

quiz.q: What does 'kurwadza kunopisa' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Kunopisa' means burning, so 'kurwadza kunopisa' means burning pain.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I cannot sleep because of the pain' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Handikwanise kurara' means 'I cannot sleep', and 'nekuda kwekurwadziwa' means 'because of the pain'.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'toothache'?
quiz.explanation: 'Zino' means tooth, and 'rinorwadza' means hurts, so 'zino rinorwadza' means toothache.

quiz.q: How do you say 'You should eat fruits' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Unofanira kudya michero' means 'You should eat fruits'.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'exercise'?
quiz.explanation: 'Kurovedza muviri' means exercise.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I wash my hands' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndinogeza maoko' means 'I wash my hands'.

quiz.q: What does 'usaputa fodya' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Usaputa fodya' means 'Don't smoke'.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I want to prevent disease' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Kudzivirira' means to prevent, and 'chirwere' means disease.

quiz.q: What is the emergency number for ambulance in Zimbabwe?
quiz.explanation: In Zimbabwe, 994 is for ambulance, 995 for fire, and 999 for police.

quiz.q: How do you shout 'Fire!' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Moto!' means fire.

quiz.q: What does 'Ndapota, ndibatsireiwo!' mean?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndapota' means please, and 'ndibatsireiwo' means help me.

quiz.q: How do you say 'He/She is bleeding' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Kubuda ropa' means bleeding.

quiz.q: What is the Shona word for 'unconscious'?
quiz.explanation: 'Akapera simba' means unconscious.

quiz.q: How do you say 'I am lost' in Shona?
quiz.explanation: 'Ndarasika' means 'I am lost'.
